findings.claim: Campaign A generates GBP 120,000 extra profit for GBP 80,000 spent (from GBP 200,000 of extra sales).
findings.truth: Extra sales minus the campaign cost is not profit - the cost of the goods sold is still to come. The lesson's own arithmetic (150% and 100%) is correct; only the label 'profit' is wrong. Revenue versus profit is examined content.

findings.claim: The UK's Advertising Standards Authority fines firms that get this wrong.
findings.truth: The ASA is a self-regulator with no power to fine. It can order adverts withdrawn, publish rulings, require pre-vetting, and refer advertisers to Trading Standards or Ofcom - it is Ofcom that can fine.

findings.claim: When BrewDog set a 2030 carbon-negative target...
findings.truth: BrewDog had no 2030 target: it claimed to be carbon negative already, and has since been winding that claim down. The example is rewritten without the invented target.

findings.claim: In 2020 Boohoo was accused of buying from Leicester suppliers paying below the minimum wage; sales fell, the share price dropped, and the company had to commission an independent review.
findings.truth: The share price fell sharply in July 2020 and the independent review followed, but Boohoo's sales carried on growing through that year. The sales claim is removed.
findings.evidence: Boohoo Group results for the year to Feb 2021

findings.claim: Vehicles in UK clean-air zones like London's ULEZ pay daily charges.
findings.truth: Only vehicles that fail the emissions standard pay. Compliant vehicles enter free.

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Give one UK business built on ethical sourcing.' Answer: Tony's Chocolonely.
findings.truth: The lesson itself calls Tony's Chocolonely a Dutch brand, so the question contradicts its own answer.

findings.claim: Costa Coffee and Greggs both sell only Fairtrade coffee in their UK cafes.
findings.truth: Greggs coffee is Fairtrade, but Costa's blend is certified by the Rainforest Alliance, not Fairtrade. A student naming Costa as a Fairtrade example would be wrong. I could not confirm this from Wikipedia or a government source, so it is left for a ruling. Options: (a) drop Costa and keep Greggs alone; (b) name Costa as a Rainforest Alliance example alongside Greggs. Recommendation: (a) - it needs no new asserted fact.
findings.evidence: no allowed source found; Wikipedia's Costa Coffee and Rainforest Alliance articles name no certifications
findings.ruling: Costa dropped (Rainforest Alliance, not Fairtrade); Greggs kept.

findings.truth: Greggs' 2019 total sales rose about 13.5% (GBP 1,167.9m against GBP 1,029.3m) and like-for-like shop sales about 9.2%. The 7.4% figure matches neither. I could not confirm the exact figure from an allowed source, so it needs a ruling. Recommendation: replace '7.4%' with '13.5%' after checking the 2019 annual results, or drop the percentage.

findings.claim: Nissan's Sunderland plant employs 7,000 people (also flashcard 12). Lesson 1 says around 6,000.
findings.truth: Sources differ: the plant's own current figure is around 6,000 direct employees, while older figures give 7,000 direct plus about 500 contracted. Not clearly wrong, but the unit contradicts itself between lesson 1 and lesson 14.

findings.claim: Margin of safety and break-even chart reading are taught as part of the break-even topic.
findings.truth: The spec names only 'the concept of break-even', 'simple calculation of break-even quantity' and 'the usefulness of break-even in decision-making'. Margin of safety and chart construction are not named, though chart interpretation falls under the quantitative skills appendix. Useful extension, not misleading - no edit.

findings.claim: Nissan chose Sunderland in the 1980s because the UK offered easy access to the EU single market.
findings.truth: The single market began in 1993 and the EU in 1993; in 1984 the draw was the European Community market. Anachronism rather than a business error, so no edit.

summary: 35 findings across all 15 lessons, 39 edits. The dominant defect is a fabricated 12-mark tariff (seven lessons, in exam tips and top-band practice questions) on a paper whose tariffs stop at 9. Every calculation in the unit - revenue, costs, gross and net profit, both margins, ARR, break-even, margin of safety and every cash-flow row - recomputes correctly, and every knowledge-check key is right; the one knowledge-check defect is a match question with two identical options that the grader compares by index. The rest are real-world statistics: the Suez blockage value, the Tesco horsemeat figure, the Toyota recall, the ASA's power to fine, Cazoo, BrewDog and Boohoo.
